eventCatalog.realSignal: NLRB representation petitions filed by coffee shop workers
eventCatalog.realFrequency: OCF Coffee House (Philadelphia) closed all shops in June 2024 after a union push; The Wydown (Washington) closed six days before its election in May 2024.
eventCatalog.note: A first contract raising pay about 8% is my estimate; no statistic for independent cafes was found.

eventCatalog.name: January 1: the minimum wage may step up
eventCatalog.text: The minimum wage is indexed to inflation and announced by October 1. For 2027 the step was cancelled by an off-ramp: $17.00 stays. In a year when it applies, every worker at or near the floor moves with it.
eventCatalog.trigger: calendar: January 1 of a year in which the Labor Department announces an increase (not 2027); announced October 1
eventCatalog.realSignal: New York State Department of Labor minimum wage order; CPI-W for the Northeast, three-year moving average
eventCatalog.realFrequency: $16.50 to $17.00 on January 1, 2026 (+3.0%). No increase on January 1, 2027.
eventCatalog.note: Seen on the NY Department of Labor page on November 14, 2026: "On January 1, 2027, New York’s minimum wage will stay the same... $17.00 per hour in New York City"; an off-ramp condition was met. The event therefore does NOT fire in January 2027. The x1.03 multiplier is for a later year in which indexing applies (3% is a projection, my estimate). The last real step was $16.50 to $17.00 on January 1, 2026.

eventCatalog.name: You are running on empty
eventCatalog.text: Nine months of opening shifts. You snap at a regular, forget an order, miss a tax notice.
eventCatalog.trigger: decision: owner_schedule "every shift" for nine months without a manager or a day off
eventCatalog.realSignal: Owner hours per week
eventCatalog.realFrequency: "Burned out" is the owner's stated reason in closings from Milwaukee (2026) to Los Angeles (2025).
eventCatalog.note: The size of the quality and reputation loss is a game-balance choice. Needs the owner-hours mechanic.

eventCatalog.name: The only certified supervisor is out sick
eventCatalog.text: Flu season. The one person holding the Food Protection Certificate - you - is in bed for a week. Open without a certificate holder and it is a violation.
eventCatalog.trigger: calendar event flu_season; hits only shops with a single Food Protection Certificate holder
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC Health Department weekly influenza surveillance report
eventCatalog.realFrequency: A certificate holder must be on site every open hour; the free online course costs $24 for the exam.
eventCatalog.note: Five days is a typical flu absence, my estimate. A second certificate costs $24 plus about 15 paid hours of study.

eventCatalog.name: The deposits do not match the register
eventCatalog.text: The bank statement is short of the daily reports, and has been for months.
eventCatalog.trigger: decision: cash_controls "none" for three months; discovered when the option changes or in month 6
eventCatalog.realSignal: Difference between register reports and bank deposits
eventCatalog.realFrequency: A New Zealand cafe lost about $25,000 in three months to an inherited manager; Good Karma Cafe in Philadelphia reported $17,000 embezzled.
eventCatalog.note: 1.5% of sales a month is my estimate: about $750 a month on $51,000 of sales, far below the two reported cases.

eventCatalog.name: A chain coffee shop opens on your block
eventCatalog.text: A "Coming soon" sign goes up 100 yards away. Cheaper drip coffee, an app, a longer lease than yours.
eventCatalog.trigger: announced two months ahead for one block
eventCatalog.realSignal: New Health Department food service permits within 250 m (DOHMH restaurant data); chain store counts
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Dunkin' has 623 shops in the city. Buddies Coffee's owner learned of a coffee shop opening next door in the months before closing (2025). A discount chain was reported to be eyeing the stores Starbucks closed in 2025.
eventCatalog.note: x0.88: one more rival among about seven within 250 m takes roughly an eighth of the same walkers. In the footfall model of the keen-cray branch the rival should simply be added to the rivals list; the multiplier is the fallback.

eventCatalog.name: The chain on your corner closes
eventCatalog.text: The chain store two blocks away is on the closure list. Its morning regulars need a new place.
eventCatalog.trigger: announced one month ahead for one block
eventCatalog.realSignal: Chain closure announcements; DOHMH permits not renewed
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Starbucks closed 42 New York City stores (12%) in September 2025; Blank Street closed its last East Village shop in August 2026.
eventCatalog.note: x1.06 is my estimate: half the gain of a rival's arrival, because a closed chain's customers scatter among all shops.

eventCatalog.name: More coffee carts on the street
eventCatalog.text: The city issues thousands of new vending licenses. A cart with $2 coffee sets up near the subway entrance on your corner.
eventCatalog.trigger: announced: 2027 licensing round
eventCatalog.realSignal: Mobile food vending permits and supervisory licenses issued by the Health Department
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Reform package: 10,700 new general vending licenses in 2027 and 2,200 food supervisory licenses a year until 2031.
eventCatalog.note: x0.96 is my estimate for take-away drip coffee lost at commuter corners; no measurement exists.

eventCatalog.name: A food account features your block
eventCatalog.text: A video of the block passes a million views. For three weeks there is a line out the door - and a hold on your card payouts while the processor reviews the spike.
eventCatalog.trigger: announced one week ahead for one block
eventCatalog.realSignal: Views of posts geotagged to the block; card volume against the business's own three-month average
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Buddies Coffee: 7 million views in February 2025, crowds for weeks, closed in May. Processors list an unexpected rise in transactions as a reason to hold funds.
eventCatalog.note: x1.3 is the engine's upper limit for an event. Payout hold: a shop whose month is more than 50% above its three-month average receives that month's card money one month late (my rule; processors publish no threshold).

eventCatalog.name: Your rating drops a star
eventCatalog.text: Slow service and a B in the window turn into one-star reviews. New customers pick the place across the street.
eventCatalog.trigger: decision: quality below 0.4 for two months, or a posted grade of B or C
eventCatalog.realSignal: Average star rating on Yelp and Google
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Harvard Business School study of Yelp and Washington State tax records: one star more means 5-9% more revenue for independent restaurants, nothing for chains.
eventCatalog.note: x0.93 is the middle of the 5-9% range for one star.

eventCatalog.name: Offices call people back
eventCatalog.text: Big employers move from three office days to four or five. Weekday mornings in office districts fill up.
eventCatalog.trigger: announced one month ahead; prime-tier blocks only
eventCatalog.realSignal: Kastle Back to Work Barometer for New York City; Partnership for New York City office survey
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Kastle: New York City peak-day occupancy of 87.3% on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, the highest since March 2020; a monthly average of 66.0%.
eventCatalog.note: x1.06 for prime-tier weekday traffic is my estimate. Card-swipe data measures buildings, not workers.

eventCatalog.name: January
eventCatalog.text: The slowest month of the coffee year. Gift cards sold in December come back as free drinks. The wage step, the quarter's sales tax and the year-end payroll filings land in the same weeks.
eventCatalog.trigger: calendar
eventCatalog.realSignal: Chain same-store sales by month; card transaction data
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year. Starbucks: December sales 58% above January (2016 card data). Restaurants: same-store sales growth -4.5% in January 2024.
eventCatalog.note: x0.88 is my estimate for an independent shop: far milder than the Starbucks holiday swing (driven by gift cards and seasonal drinks), stronger than the restaurant-wide -4.5%.

eventCatalog.name: Laptop season
eventCatalog.text: It is cold outside and warm inside. Half your tables hold one person, one laptop and one drink bought at 9am.
eventCatalog.trigger: calendar; hits shops with wifi_policy "open"
eventCatalog.realSignal: Average minutes per seated customer; orders per seat per day
eventCatalog.realFrequency: New York shops now limit Wi-Fi to two hours on weekdays and switch it off on weekends (Devocion), or confine laptops to one room (Sweetleaf).
eventCatalog.note: x0.85 on unitsServedPerSizeMonth is my estimate; no dwell-time data for cafes was found. The engine has no seat-turnover effect target yet.

eventCatalog.name: Tax warrant and seizure
eventCatalog.text: Two quarters of sales tax unpaid. The state files a warrant, posts a SEIZED notice and changes the locks.
eventCatalog.trigger: decision: shortcut keep_sales_tax (from the common pack) active across two quarterly due dates
eventCatalog.realSignal: New York State tax warrants filed against the business
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Vox Pop, Brooklyn: seized December 2009 and April 2010 over $66,000; assets auctioned.
eventCatalog.note: Two missed quarters before a seizure and 30 closed days are my simplification; the real sequence is notice, warrant, levy. Quarterly returns are due March 20, June 20, September 20 and December 20.

eventCatalog.name: Workers' compensation audit
eventCatalog.text: The insurer audits last year's payroll. You paid more wages than you estimated; here is the bill for the difference.
eventCatalog.trigger: calendar: month 14 after opening (after the first policy year)
eventCatalog.realSignal: Actual payroll against the payroll estimated on the policy
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every policy year for every employer.
eventCatalog.note: If payroll ran 20% over the estimate, the extra premium is 20% of a premium of about 2% of payroll = 0.4% of annual payroll, about $650 on $165,000. Falls after a 12-month season: belongs in the personal plan.

eventCatalog.name: "Cash in 24 hours"
eventCatalog.text: A broker calls every week in January: $40,000 tomorrow, repaid as a share of each day's card sales.
eventCatalog.trigger: announced: offered to every business whose cash is under two months of fixed costs
eventCatalog.realSignal: Factor rate and daily holdback in merchant cash advance agreements
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Court record: 35% of a Manhattan restaurant's card receipts every weekday until $145,000 was collected (2019). A $100,000 advance is typically repaid as $140,000-$150,000.
eventCatalog.note: Game terms: $40,000 advanced, $56,000 repaid (factor 1.4, the low end of the quoted range), 15% of card sales held back daily - milder than the 35% in the court case so that the choice is not an instant loss.

eventCatalog.name: Accessibility lawsuit
eventCatalog.text: A federal complaint arrives: one step at the entrance, no ramp. The plaintiff has filed dozens like it this year.
eventCatalog.trigger: decision: a place with a step at the door and no ramp (setup item portable_ramp not bought), month 8 after opening
eventCatalog.realSignal: ADA Title III complaints filed in the Southern and Eastern Districts of New York
eventCatalog.realFrequency: One plaintiffs' firm has filed about 600 such suits in New York federal courts; coffee shops and breweries are named targets.
eventCatalog.note: $10,000 covers a settlement and your own lawyer; published ranges ($5,000-$25,000) come from vendor blogs and are not verified. Needs the private-claims mechanic and a place attribute "step at entrance".

eventCatalog.name: A letter from a music rights society
eventCatalog.text: A licensing agent sat in your shop for an hour and wrote down the songs. Pay for a license and for the months already played.
eventCatalog.trigger: decision: shortcut personal_playlist active for six months
eventCatalog.realSignal: Licensing demand letters from ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, GMR
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Statutory damages for willful infringement reach $150,000 a work; small-shop licenses run a few hundred dollars a year per society.
eventCatalog.note: $1,500 = about two societies at $350 for the current year plus the back year; my estimate of a settled letter, not a court award.

eventCatalog.name: Pay-frequency claim
eventCatalog.text: A former barista's lawyer writes: manual workers must be paid weekly, and you paid every two weeks.
eventCatalog.trigger: decision: shortcut biweekly_pay active for six months
eventCatalog.realSignal: Labor Law §191 complaints and class actions
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Class actions became common after a 2019 appellate ruling; the May 2025 amendment limits a first violation to interest.
eventCatalog.note: First violation: interest at 16% a year on wages paid a week late = about 0.3% of the late wages. A repeat violation costs 100% of the late-paid wages.

eventCatalog.name: The neighborhood wants to save you
eventCatalog.text: Regulars offer to start a fundraiser. The money is real, and so is the question of what it changes.
eventCatalog.trigger: decision: available once, when cash is under one month of fixed costs and reputation is above 0.6
eventCatalog.realSignal: Crowdfunding campaigns for restaurants and cafes
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Boris & Horton raised $250,000 in February 2024 and ran out of money by the end of that year; a Florida cafe raised $2,000 for a grease trap.
eventCatalog.note: Half a month of revenue is a game-balance value. If the business closes within six months of a campaign its owner's reliability score takes the hit.

eventCatalog.name: Coffee falls on the exchange
eventCatalog.text: Arabica futures are a third below last year's peak. Your roaster's price list moves down slowly.
eventCatalog.trigger: announced
eventCatalog.realSignal: ICE Coffee C front-month futures against the six-month average
eventCatalog.realFrequency: About $4.23 a pound on November 11, 2025 and about $2.80 on November 6, 2026.
eventCatalog.note: A 34% fall in green coffee, passed on by half, on beans at about 25% of cost of goods = -4%; shown as x0.98 because roasters lag (my estimate).

eventCatalog.name: World Cup summer
eventCatalog.text: Eight matches across the river, the final on July 19. Hotels are full. Fan zones and bars with screens are packed; a quiet block sees an ordinary summer.
eventCatalog.trigger: calendar: June 11 - July 19, 2026; prime-tier blocks only
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC Tourism visitor counts and hotel revenue
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Hotel room revenue up 20.6% year on year; the city rewards program logged about 10,000 visits across 1,000+ small businesses.
eventCatalog.note: x1.05 in the prime tier only is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: Marathon Sunday
eventCatalog.text: First Sunday of November: the course runs through all five boroughs. Blocks on the route are closed to cars and lined with spectators from 8am.
eventCatalog.trigger: calendar: November 1, 2026; blocks on the course
eventCatalog.realSignal: TCS New York City Marathon course map and road closure schedule
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Yearly; November 1, 2026 was the 50th running of the five-borough course.
eventCatalog.note: One day at double traffic = +3% of the month on route blocks; deliveries cannot reach the shop that morning.

eventCatalog.name: A neighbor complains about the back yard
eventCatalog.text: Someone upstairs calls 311 about the tables in your yard. The Buildings Department orders the space vacated.
eventCatalog.trigger: decision: shortcut backyard_seating active; found by a complaint or an inspection like any other violation
eventCatalog.realSignal: DOB complaints and partial vacate orders
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Yaffa Cafe, East Village: a 100-seat garden used for three decades, vacated after one neighbor's complaint in 2014; the cafe closed weeks later.
eventCatalog.note: Fits the game's "report to the city" attack: see report_illegal_seating.

eventCatalog.name: December gift cards come home
eventCatalog.text: The gift cards you sold before the holidays are being spent. Cups go out; no money comes in.
eventCatalog.trigger: decision: lever gift_cards "push in December"
eventCatalog.realSignal: Gift card liability on the balance sheet
eventCatalog.realFrequency: New York gift cards cannot expire for nine years and can be cashed out under $5.
eventCatalog.note: 6% of December sales moved from January-February cash into December is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: Rolling reserve on card payouts
eventCatalog.text: After two chargebacks in a month the processor starts keeping part of every day's card sales in reserve.
eventCatalog.trigger: decision: refund_policy "no refunds" for three months
eventCatalog.realSignal: Chargeback ratio on the merchant account
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Processors describe holds (payouts paused) and reserves (a percentage kept back) as tools against chargeback risk.
eventCatalog.note: 10% of card sales held for 90 days is my estimate; reports from 2020 mention up to 30% for 120 days.

eventCatalog.name: Workers stay home

mechanics.title: Closed, and the rent still runs
mechanics.playerDecision: Before: all-electric or gas kitchen, a second certificate holder, labor shortcuts on or off, sales tax paid or spent. During: wait, or (water only) stay open illegally.
mechanics.engineMath: A business can be closed by an event or by its own decisions, not only by an inspector. While closed: served = 0, rent and fixed monthlyCosts are charged in full, hourly staff are not paid after day 3 (they leave: staff count resets to minStaff and training is paid again on reopening), demand on reopening is multiplied by (1 - 0.01 x closed days), floor 0.6, and recovers through the awareness ramp. Sources of closure: gas_red_tag (months), water_off (days), staff_walkout (16 days), flu_takes_the_only_supervisor (5 days), sales_tax_warrant (30 days).

mechanics.title: The lease has an end date
mechanics.playerDecision: At signing: term and renewal option (lever lease_terms), with or without the free lease review. At the renewal letter: accept the new rent, move (pay a new build-out and lose most regulars), or close.
mechanics.engineMath: Every business stores leaseEndMonth. Six months before it the engine sends the renewal offer: newRent = max(contract rent x 1.03^years, market asking rent of the place tier x sqft / 12) without an option; contract rent x 1.03 with an option. A sold building (block event) removes the offer for businesses without an option. Leaving early: the owner owes rent until the landlord re-lets, capped by the deposit plus the guaranty months. In a 12-month season the clock matters for (a) takeovers of the tail of an existing lease - cheaper entry, renewal inside the season - and (b) the personal plan at season end, which prints the renewal risk in dollars.

A full timeline, in months, of a commercial nonpayment eviction in New York City.
Price of utility-interruption and spoilage endorsements for a small cafe policy.
A New York City coffee shop that closed permanently after a Health Department closure with the owner saying so (only reopenings were found).
A New York cafe closure caused by a wage lawsuit, and one caused by a break-in series (found only outside New York).

levers.name: Lease terms (chosen when you sign)

options.label: Ten years with a renewal option at fixed 3% yearly steps; one more month of deposit and a longer negotiation
Take over the last years of someone else's lease

levers.note: The option decides what events lease_renewal_offer and building_sold can do to you. $1,500 is extra lawyer time, my estimate. Commercial tenants in New York have no statutory right to renew; an option exists only if it is written into the lease.

levers.name: Kitchen energy (chosen at build-out)

options.label: All electric: espresso, oven, water heater
Gas water heater and range: cheaper to run, more permits

levers.note: Gas is assumed to save 10% of the $1,100 utilities line; my estimate, not a tariff comparison. A gas shop is exposed to the gas_red_tag event; an all-electric shop is not.

levers.name: Repair and slow-season reserve
levers.note: Not an expense: the money moves to a reserve the business still owns (see mechanic reserve_fund). Amounts are 1% and 3% of the reference month's $51,000 of sales. One-off bills (repairs, audit, tax escalation, claims) are paid from the reserve first.

levers.name: Second keyholder and second certificate

options.label: Only you hold the keys and the Food Protection Certificate
Train a lead: second certificate, keys, opening and closing

levers.note: $160 a month = a $1 an hour lead premium x 140 hours + the $24 exam and about 15 paid study hours ($255) spread over a year. Protects against flu_takes_the_only_supervisor and softens key_barista_leaves and owner_burnout.

levers.name: Your own hours behind the bar

options.label: Open and close every day yourself

levers.note: Negative cost = barista wages you do not pay: $3,360 a month is one barista at 140 hours and $17 plus employer taxes as the engine prices it; half of that for half the shifts. Nine months of "every shift" triggers owner_burnout.

levers.name: Cash and bank controls

options.label: Trust the team; look at the bank balance now and then
Count the drawer every night, match deposits weekly (your time)
Bookkeeper reconciles register, bank and payroll every week

levers.note: $200 a month on top of the pack's $400 bookkeeping line is my estimate. "owner_daily" costs no money but counts as owner hours.

levers.name: Wi-Fi and laptops

options.label: Open Wi-Fi, stay as long as you like
Two-hour Wi-Fi code with a purchase
No Wi-Fi; no laptops on weekends

levers.note: Effect sizes are game-balance values. Real policies: Devocion limits Wi-Fi to two hours on weekdays and switches it off on weekends.

levers.name: Insurance add-ons

options.label: Add utility interruption, spoilage and equipment breakdown

levers.note: $40 a month is my estimate; no price list was found. Typical utility-services sublimits are $2,500-$25,000. With the add-on, summer_outage costs only the deductible.

levers.name: Music
levers.note: $35 a month is my estimate of a bundled business streaming plan; direct licenses from ASCAP and BMI start at roughly $250-$415 a year each (vendor-quoted). The illegal option is shortcut personal_playlist.

levers.name: Sign on the sidewalk
levers.note: +2% demand is a game-balance value. Sanitation fines: $100 first, up to $300 after (figures reported in 2015).

levers.name: Sales that do not need the sidewalk

options.label: Office coffee boxes, catering trays and bags of beans

levers.note: $300 a month for packaging and deliveries and +4% demand are my estimates. This demand is not multiplied by foot-traffic events (street_dig, barricades, sidewalk shed).

levers.name: Gift cards
levers.note: Moves cash from January-February into December; see gift_card_hangover.

levers.name: Complaints and refunds
levers.note: $250 a month = about 0.5% of sales in remade drinks, my estimate.

levers.name: End-of-day pastry

options.label: Sell surprise bags through a surplus-food app

levers.note: -$300 a month (income) is my estimate: three bags a day at about $5 after the app's cut, 22 days. The app's own example: a two-shop New York bakery cafe earned $66,576 (period not stated).

levers.name: Yearly harassment-prevention training

options.label: One paid hour per worker a year with the state's free model training

levers.note: $6 a month = four workers x one paid hour at $17 / 12. New York State requires every employer to train every worker each year and offers a free model course; the requirement itself is from my knowledge of the law and was not re-checked in this session.

shortcuts.name: Pay baristas every two weeks
shortcuts.what: One payroll run instead of two saves the run fee and a week of float. New York says manual workers are paid weekly.

shortcuts.name: Play your own streaming playlist
shortcuts.what: A personal music account is not licensed for a shop. Saves the business plan fee until a rights society notices.

shortcuts.name: Add a 3% card fee at the register
shortcuts.what: Customers pay your processing fee. Legal only if the card price itself is posted and the fee is no more than your processor charges.

shortcuts.name: Seat customers in the back yard
shortcuts.what: Twelve more seats without a filing at the Buildings Department. One complaint from a neighbor ends it.

shortcuts.name: Stay open while the water is off
shortcuts.what: No running water means no handwashing and no dishwashing. Closing for the day costs a day of sales.

shortcuts.name: Leave the step at the door as it is
shortcuts.what: A portable ramp and a bell cost a few hundred dollars. Without them the shop is a ready-made accessibility lawsuit.

violations.name: Manual workers not paid weekly
violations.law: NY Labor Law §191(1)(a); §198(1-a) as amended May 9, 2025
violations.note: First violation by an employer who paid at least twice a month: interest only (16% a year, about 0.3% of the late wages). Half of a $13,456 monthly payroll is paid a week late: about $20 a month. A repeat violation owes 100% of the late-paid wages as liquidated damages - the engine should switch to perMonth = half the monthly payroll on the second finding.

violations.name: Music played without a public performance license
violations.note: Not a city fine: a rights society sends an agent, then a demand letter. $1,500 is my estimate of a settled letter (two licenses plus the back year); statutory damages for willful infringement reach $150,000 a work.

violations.name: Card surcharge not posted as a price
violations.note: Up to $500 per violation. The pack charges one violation per finding; a real enforcement action can count each transaction or each day.

violations.name: A-frame sign blocking the sidewalk
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-118; Department of Sanitation rules
violations.note: $100 for a first sign violation and up to $300 after, as a Sanitation spokesperson told the Midtown Gazette (2015 enforcement). The current schedule was not found.

violations.name: Back yard used for seating contrary to the Certificate of Occupancy
violations.note: The section exists; the current penalty amount was NOT found. $1,250 is the default penalty of a Class 2 violation in an older schedule and stands here as a placeholder. The real cost is the vacate order: the seats are gone (event garden_complaint).

violations.name: Operating without hot and cold running water
violations.law: NYC Health Code §81.20; 24 RCNY Chapter 23 (public health hazard)
violations.note: The penalty schedule lists inadequate potable water as a public health hazard; the dollar amount for running without hot and cold water was NOT found, $400 is a placeholder at the level of the pack's other health fines. An uncorrected public health hazard closes the shop.

violations.name: Entrance not accessible
violations.law: Americans with Disabilities Act Title III, 42 U.S.C. §12182; NYC Human Rights Law
violations.note: A private lawsuit, not an inspection. $10,000 = settlement plus your own lawyer, my estimate inside the unverified $5,000-$25,000 range quoted by vendors.

officials.name: Sanitation enforcement agent
officials.realProcess: Agents walk commercial streets on set routes and write summonses for dirty sidewalks, bags without bins, late set-out and sidewalk obstructions. Summonses are answered at OATH.

officials.name: Buildings inspector
officials.realProcess: Answers 311 complaints about illegal use, unpermitted work and signs. Can issue a violation and a partial vacate order for a space used contrary to the Certificate of Occupancy.

officials.name: Private plaintiff
officials.agency: Civil court (no city agency: a person or a rights society sues)
officials.realProcess: A tester or licensing agent visits like any customer, documents the problem and sends a demand letter or files suit. Most cases settle for less than the cost of a defense.

reports.name: Report illegal seating or use (311, Buildings)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint to the Department of Buildings about a back yard, basement or roof used without approval. An inspector visits; an illegal space is ordered vacated. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a blocked sidewalk (311, Sanitation)
reports.text: In real life: a 311 complaint about an A-frame sign or other obstruction on the sidewalk. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

reports.name: Report a hidden card fee (Consumer Protection)
reports.text: In real life: a complaint about a surcharge added at checkout that was not posted as a price. If you are wrong, you get a warning.

setup.name: Portable ramp, door bell and accessibility sign
setup.note: $300 is my estimate of a folding threshold ramp, a wireless bell and a sign; no price list was opened. Removes the access_claim event for a place with one step. A permanent ramp needs an architect and a Buildings filing.

setup.name: Health Department consultative inspection (before the first graded one)
setup.note: From the permit application packet as returned by search: $100 for a consultative inspection requested after opening and before the first graded inspection; $400 for one requested later. No grade and no fines are issued. Number seen in a search summary, page not opened.

setup.name: Free lease review (NYC Small Business Services)
setup.agency: NYC Department of Small Business Services
setup.note: The city offers free commercial lease help to small businesses; this item is the in-game hook that reveals the lease's renewal, termination and tax-escalation clauses before signing.

monthlyCosts.name: Licensed background music
monthlyCosts.note: My estimate of a bundled business music plan. Direct licenses from ASCAP and BMI start at roughly $250-$415 a year each for a small room (vendor-quoted).

monthlyCosts.name: Hiring and training replacements
monthlyCosts.note: Annual turnover of 50% x $2,500 to replace one hourly worker (middle of the $1,500-$3,500 range) / 12 = $104 per worker a month. Trade figures, not a survey of New York.

monthlyCosts.name: Unsold pastry thrown out
monthlyCosts.note: My estimate: pastry is about a fifth of sales, bought at half the menu price, and about one in ten pieces is left at closing: 0.2 x 0.5 x 0.1 = 1% of sales. The pack's cost of goods already includes "spoilage" inside its 26%, so this line should be split out of it, not added.

events.name: January
events.text: The slowest month of the coffee year, with the wage step and the quarter's sales tax due around it.
events.note: Starbucks: December 58% above January (2016 card data); restaurants -4.5% in January 2024. x0.88 is my estimate for an independent shop.

events.name: A chain coffee shop opens on your block
events.text: One more place selling coffee to the same walkers.
events.note: One more rival among about seven within 250 m. Block-level event.

events.name: The street is torn up
events.text: A water main replacement fences off the block for most of a year.
events.note: Owners on Second Avenue reported sales down 20-50% during subway construction.

events.name: January 1: the minimum wage may step up
events.text: The minimum wage is indexed to inflation and announced by October 1. For 2027 the step was cancelled by an off-ramp: $17.00 stays. In a year when it applies, every worker at or near the floor moves with it.
events.note: Seen on the NY Department of Labor page on November 14, 2026: "On January 1, 2027, New York’s minimum wage will stay the same... $17.00 per hour in New York City"; an off-ramp condition was met. The event therefore does NOT fire in January 2027. The x1.03 multiplier is for a later year in which indexing applies (3% is a projection, my estimate). The last real step was $16.50 to $17.00 on January 1, 2026.

events.name: Offices call people back
events.text: Weekday mornings fill up in office districts.
events.note: Kastle: peak-day occupancy 87.3% in New York City on October 27, 2026. Prime tier only.

events.name: Your rating drops a star
events.text: One star less on review sites costs an independent restaurant 5-9% of revenue.
events.note: Luca (Harvard Business School): one star = 5-9% of revenue for independents. Triggered by the player's own quality, not by chance.

events.name: Sidewalk shed goes up on your block
events.text: Scaffolding covers your storefront while the building repairs its facade. The average shed in the city has stood for a year and a half.
events.note: CORRECTION of the existing event (same id): months 3 -> 12. Average shed age: 509 days in May 2025 (8,559 sheds), 557 days in March 2026. Twelve months is the cap of a season. The 10% drop stays an estimate.

ruleCards.title: Your lease ends when it ends
ruleCards.text: A commercial tenant in New York has no right to renew and no cap on the next rent. In 2025 Brooklyn cafes were offered two to three times their old rent. An option to renew exists only if it is written into the lease.

ruleCards.title: Gas comes back slowly
ruleCards.text: After a utility shuts off a building's gas, service returns only after a licensed plumber, a Buildings permit, a pressure test and an inspection. One Brooklyn cafe was dark for more than 8 months over a $3,000 repair.

ruleCards.title: Sidewalk sheds
ruleCards.text: The city had 8,559 sidewalk sheds in May 2025 with an average age of 509 days. The building puts the shed up; a standard lease gives the tenant no rent relief.

ruleCards.title: Weekly pay
ruleCards.text: New York manual workers - more than 25% of the time on physical tasks - must be paid weekly. A first offender who paid twice a month owes interest; a repeat offender owes 100% of the late wages.

ruleCards.title: Music is licensed
ruleCards.text: A personal streaming account does not cover a shop. Public performance needs licenses from ASCAP, BMI, SESAC and GMR or a business music service. Statutory damages for willful infringement reach $150,000 a work.

ruleCards.title: Card fees must be posted as prices
ruleCards.text: Since February 11, 2024 a New York seller that charges more for cards must post the card price (or both prices) and may not add more than its processor charges. Penalty: up to $500 per violation.

ruleCards.title: The A-frame sign
ruleCards.text: A sign standing on the sidewalk is an obstruction. Sanitation tickets have run $100 for a first sign and up to $300 after.

ruleCards.title: Space you may not use
ruleCards.text: A yard, basement or roof not covered by the Certificate of Occupancy can be ordered vacated after a single complaint. Yaffa Cafe lost a 100-seat garden it had used for 30 years.

ruleCards.title: No water, no service
ruleCards.text: A food business needs hot and cold running water every open minute. Without it the Health Department treats the shop as a public health hazard and can close it on the spot.

ruleCards.title: The step at the door
ruleCards.text: One step at the entrance is enough for a federal accessibility lawsuit. One plaintiffs' firm has filed about 600 in New York; coffee shops are frequent targets. Settling usually costs less than defending.

ruleCards.title: Sales tax seizure
ruleCards.text: For unpaid sales tax New York files a warrant and can seize the business: a notice on the door, new locks, an auction. A Brooklyn cafe was padlocked twice over $66,000. Returns are due March 20, June 20, September 20 and December 20.

ruleCards.title: Buying a business: the bulk sale notice
ruleCards.text: A buyer of a business files Form AU-196.10 with the Tax Department at least 10 days before paying or taking possession. Skip it and the seller's unpaid sales tax can be collected from you.

ruleCards.title: Merchant cash advance
ruleCards.text: An advance is repaid as a share of every day's card sales. Court records show 35% of a restaurant's receipts taken daily until $145,000 was collected. A $100,000 advance is commonly repaid as $140,000-$150,000.

ruleCards.title: Power outages and insurance
ruleCards.text: A standard policy excludes a power failure that starts off your premises. Lost sales and spoiled stock are paid only with a utility-services endorsement and spoilage coverage, often limited to $2,500-$25,000.

ruleCards.title: Fines can be erased
ruleCards.text: Score under 14 points on re-inspection and the penalties from that inspection are waived. New restaurants can book a consultative visit with no grade and no fines: $100 before the first graded inspection.

ruleCards.title: Protected time off, 2026
ruleCards.text: Since February 22, 2026 every New York City employer owes each worker 32 unpaid hours a year from day one, on top of 40 paid hours, plus 20 hours of paid prenatal leave. Paid and unpaid balances are tracked separately.

ruleCards.title: Wage indexing
ruleCards.text: The minimum wage is indexed to Northeast inflation from 2027, with off-ramps. For 2027 an off-ramp was met: the rate stays $17.00 in New York City on January 1, 2027. The next rate is announced by October 1 each year.

ruleCards.title: Pre-opening costs and tax
ruleCards.text: Only $5,000 of start-up costs is deductible in the first year, and nothing at once when they exceed $55,000. The rest is spread over 180 months. Rent paid before opening day is a start-up cost.

ruleCards.title: Bins, not bags
ruleCards.text: Since March 1, 2024 every business that sets trash on the curb must use bins with secure lids. Fines: $50, $100, then $200. Sidewalk and 18 inches of gutter must be kept clean.

ruleCards.title: Skip the Stuff
ruleCards.text: Since July 31, 2023 take-out and delivery orders may not include utensils, napkins or condiment packets unless the customer asks. Fines: $50, $150, then $250 within 12 months.

ruleCards.title: The first year is not the dangerous one
ruleCards.text: A study of 81,000 independent restaurants found 17% failed in year one - not 90%. An Ohio study found 26% in year one and 59% within three years: shops die when the opening money is gone.
